context.caption: RETRO incorporates information retrieved from a database to free its parameters from being an expensive store of facts and world knowledge.
context.heading: Video
context.before: This article breaks down DeepMind’s RETRO (Retrieval-Enhanced TRansfOrmer) and how it works. The model performs on par with GPT-3 despite being 4% its size (7.5 billion parameters vs. 185 billion for GPT-3 Da Vinci).
context.after: RETRO was presented in the paper Improving Language Models by Retrieving from Trillions of Tokens. It continues and builds on a wide variety of retrieval work in the research community. This article explains the model and not what is especially novel about it.

context.caption: Aiding language models with retrieval methods allows us to reduce the amount of information a language model needs to encode in its parameters to perform well at text generation.
context.heading: Why This is Important: Separating Language Information from World Knowledge Information
context.before: By including a retrieval method in the language model, the model can be much smaller. A neural database aids it with retrieving factual information it needs during text generation.
context.after: Training becomes fast with small language models, as training data memorization is reduced. Anyone can deploy these models on smaller and more affordable GPUs and tweak them as per need.

context.caption: RETRO utilizes a database to augment its input prompt. The prompt is used to retrieve relevant information from the database.
context.heading: Why This is Important: Separating Language Information from World Knowledge Information
context.before: Mechanically, RETRO is an encoder-decoder model just like the original transformer. However, it augments the input sequence with the help of a retrieval database. The model finds the most probable sequences in the database and adds them to the input. RETRO works its magic to generate the output prediction.
context.after: Before we explore the model architecture, let’s dig deeper into the retrieval database.

context.caption: A look inside RETRO's database shows examples of key-value pairs in the RETRO database. The value contains a neighbor chunk and a completion chunk.
context.heading: Inspecting RETRO’s Retrieval Database
context.before: RETRO’s database contains 2 trillion multi-lingual tokens based on the MassiveText dataset. Both the neighbor and completion chunks are at most 64 tokens long.
context.after: RETRO breaks the input prompt into multiple chunks. For simplicity, we’ll focus on how one chunk is augmented with retrieved text. The model, however, does this process for each chunk (except the first) in the input prompt.

context.caption: Processing the input prompt with BERT produces contextualized token embeddings. Averaging them produces a sentence embedding.
context.heading: The Database Lookup
context.before: Before hitting RETRO, the input prompt goes into BERT. The output contextualized vectors are then averaged to construct a sentence embedding vector. That vector is then used to query the database.
context.after: That sentence embedding is then used in an approximate nearest neighbor search (https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/scann).

context.caption: The BERT sentence embedding is used to retrieve the nearest neighbors from RETRO's neural database. These are then added to the input of the language model.
context.heading: The Database Lookup
context.before: The two nearest neighbors are retrieved, and their text becomes a part of the input into RETRO.
context.after: This is now the input to RETRO. The input prompt and its two nearest neighbors from the database (and their continuations).

context.caption: The retrieved neighbors are added to the input of the language model. They're treated a little differently inside the model, however.
context.heading: The Database Lookup
context.before: From here, the Transformer and RETRO Blocks incorporate the information into their processing.
context.after: RETRO’s architecture is an encoder stack and a decoder stack.
